extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in media, politics, public relations, journalism, and media literacy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and examples describing what 'spin' is, common spin techniques used in public relations and politics, and factors that enable or reduce the effectiveness of spin. Useful for identifying, analysing, or producing spun messages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of spin
rubrics_metrics.description: Spin is a form of propaganda achieved through knowingly providing a biased interpretation of an event; it often implies the use of disingenuous, deceptive, and manipulative tactics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spin differs from ordinary PR/advertising by its implication of deliberate deception. It is often practised by paid media advisors, pollsters and media consultants ("spin doctors").

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of press conferences / 'spin rooms' to control messaging
rubrics_metrics.description: Public figures use press conferences to control timing and specificity of messages; press conference facilities may be used as 'spin rooms' to manage media exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Controlling the venue and timing lets communicators shape which details get emphasized and when news breaks—useful both legitimately and for spinning bad news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reframing / modifying perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Reframe or modify the perception of an issue or event to reduce negative impact on public opinion (e.g., criticise competitors or highlight category-wide risks to deflect attention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often paired with catchy slogans or sound bites to persuade the public toward a biased point of view; enables refocusing attention away from negatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cherry-picking / selective presentation of facts and quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Selectively present facts and quotes that support one's position while ignoring contrary evidence ("cherry picking").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a pharmaceutical company citing only trials with positive results and ignoring many unsuccessful trials; a political staffer handpicking short quotations from past speeches to suggest support for a position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-denial denial
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement that appears to deny an accusation but in fact does not explicitly do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to create the impression of rebuttal while avoiding direct contradiction or liability; an anti-pattern for truthful, clear communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-apology apology
rubrics_metrics.description: A purported apology that lacks genuine remorse (an apology in form but not in substance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common spin tactic to pacify critics without accepting responsibility; look for absence of actor/admission and concrete corrective action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distancing language / passive voice ('Mistakes were made')
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of phrasing that acknowledges a problem while evading direct responsibility by omitting the actor (commonly via passive voice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with active voice which assigns responsibility ("I made mistakes"); distancing language is a red flag for evasive messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burying bad news (timing to minimize coverage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Announcing unpopular or damaging information at times when media attention is low (e.g., late on a workday or before a long weekend) to reduce coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sometimes combined with intentionally supplying other news to distract; timing is a deliberate tactic to limit visibility and scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misdirection and diversion (leaking competing stories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Leak or seed a different story to the media to divert attention from a more damaging story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: leaking an unrelated but newsworthy item to limit coverage of a scandal. This is an intentional redirection strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited hangout
rubrics_metrics.description: Partially reveal information (an apparent concession) while concealing more damaging truths behind it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Espionage-origin term; strategy is to appear transparent while managing how much is disclosed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewarding amenable journalists with favourable stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide exclusive stories or favourable access to journalists who are likely to produce supportive coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Builds relationships that can bias reporting; be alert to patterns of preferential access influencing coverage balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preventing access to unfavourable journalists or outlets
rubrics_metrics.description: Deny or restrict access to journalists or broadcasters who report critically, and instead give interviews to friendlier outlets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to shape the media ecosystem and avoid challenging questions; a sign of manipulative media relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dead cat strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce a sensational or shocking topic to distract public and media attention from an unwanted subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Named metaphorically; tactic relies on shock/value of diversion rather than substantive rebuttal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Astroturfing
rubrics_metrics.description: Create the appearance of grassroots support (fake grassroots campaigns) to manufacture popularity or legitimacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can involve fake organizations, coordinated messaging, or paid actors; undermines authentic public sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Big lie
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeat an enormous falsehood with such confidence and frequency that people accept it as true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A propaganda technique that leverages repetition and scale; highly deceptive and corrosive to factual discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doublespeak
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of deliberately ambiguous, euphemistic, or misleading language to disguise true meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes euphemisms and jargon that obscure responsibility or harm; signals intent to mislead rather than inform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fake or misleading testimonials / edited customer stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Produce or edit customer testimonials to give a falsely positive impression of a product or company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FTC has issued guidance and enforcement against deceptive endorsements; check for undisclosed material connections and editing that alters meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposely leaking misinformation about opponents
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberately release false or misleading information about an opposing politician or candidate to cast them negatively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A deliberate disinformation tactic; distinguish from legitimate investigative leaks that reveal verified facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spin doctors / media consultants as producers of deceptive messaging
rubrics_metrics.description: PR advisors, pollsters and media consultants who develop deceptive or misleading messages may be labelled 'spin doctors' or 'spinmeisters'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spin can be a contracted service or done in-house; awareness of the role of such actors helps analyse source motives and incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural enablers of spin (24-hour news cycle, PR reliance, advertising incentives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors that increase the prevalence and effectiveness of spin: 24-hour news pressures, journalists' reliance on PR for stories, and advertising-driven commercial pressures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When media outlets prioritize constant content and revenue, they become more susceptible to packaged or spun narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet / activism as a counterforce to spin
rubrics_metrics.description: The Internet and immediate online activism can reduce the effectiveness of spin by providing rapid counterpoints and alternative sources of information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Digital channels enable quick fact-checking and dissemination of counter-evidence, though they also enable new avenues for disinformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing electoral impact of spin
rubrics_metrics.description: Spin can influence electoral outcomes through mechanisms like targeted media endorsement and agenda-setting, though its exact effect is contested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical examples (e.g., 1997 UK election coverage and newspaper endorsements) show potential influence; measurement requires careful causal study.
